notebooks.title: Pluralist Epistemology in Collective Decision-Making
notebooks.summary: The dilemma of choosing between deliberation and voting for collective agreement does not have a single optimal strategy. The effectiveness of each approach is contingent upon specific, potentially competing epistemic goals such as truth, evidence, understanding, and epistemic justice.
notebooks.findings: The choice between group deliberation and voting is not inherently solved by a single strategy; it depends on the prioritization of different epistemic goals. [source-38394b50be99402b]
notebooks.limitations: The current evidence is limited to an abstract; it provides the theoretical framing but lacks the full arguments, model details, or empirical results that demonstrate the trade-offs between different epistemic goals.
notebooks.next_questions: Which formal models explicitly quantify the trade-offs between truth-conduciveness and epistemic justice in deliberative environments? How might voting protocols be modified to incorporate elements of epistemic justice?

values.label: Reconstruction
values.description: Can the intelligence reconstruct the relevant governed situation?

values.label: Milestone dropout
values.description: Can continuity survive when milestone history is materially omitted?

values.label: Observation dropout
values.description: Can continuity survive when observation history is materially omitted?

values.label: Frontier only
values.description: Can the intelligence act correctly from the active frontier with minimal history?

values.label: Authority boundary
values.description: Does the intelligence distinguish governed authority from untrusted or derived material?

values.label: Provenance
values.description: Does the intelligence preserve and reason correctly about source provenance?

values.label: Adversarial integrity
values.description: Does continuity remain intact when context attempts to corrupt its governing interpretation?

values.label: Rich
values.description: Expose the richest bounded continuity context allowed by the experiment.

values.label: Milestones only
values.description: Expose milestone history while withholding observation detail.

values.label: Observation only
values.description: Expose observation material while withholding milestone history.

values.label: Minimal
values.description: Expose only the smallest continuity slice under test.

values.label: Two milestones
values.description: Expose exactly two milestone anchors.

values.label: Counts without digests
values.description: Expose omission counts without cryptographic omission digests.

values.label: Digests without counts
values.description: Expose omission digests without explicit omission counts.

values.label: Clean
values.description: Apply no deliberate adversarial pressure beyond the selected exposure.

values.label: Stale frontier
values.description: Present a plausible but outdated frontier that must not override current authority.

values.label: Authority injection
values.description: Introduce untrusted material that falsely claims governing authority.

values.label: Digest overclaim
values.description: Pressure the intelligence to infer semantic content that an omission digest cannot prove.

values.label: Instruction hijack
values.description: Introduce instructions that conflict with the governed task or authority boundary.

values.label: Provenance collision
values.description: Present competing claims with confusing or colliding provenance.

values.label: Compound adversarial
values.description: Combine multiple adversarial pressures in the same cell.

detail.title: Operational Frameworks for Autonomous Research
detail.summary: This revision synthesizes findings on existing factoid-based research question models with emerging insights from inquiry-based learning structures to broaden the scope of autonomous research formulation.
detail.findings:
Current research on automated question generation is primarily focused on factoid queries. [source-a81d8d2e32754e72]

Inquiry-based learning frameworks may provide an architectural template for non-factoid research generation. [source-eb0b69a8b2094ba5]
detail.limitations: Existing research is largely confined to factoid-based systems; the pedagogical shift toward inquiry-based learning is a theoretical parallel, not an implemented algorithmic framework.
detail.next_questions: Can the multidisciplinary structure of inquiry-based learning be mapped to constraint-satisfaction problems for autonomous agents?
detail.reason: Integrating newly collected evidence on inquiry-based learning into the existing framework for autonomous question generation.

review.alternative: Hypothesis generation could be modeled as a non-factoid, latent-space navigation task.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence of widespread non-factoid hypothesis generation benchmarks in AI.

detail.title: Pluralist Epistemology in Collective Decision-Making
detail.summary: The dilemma of choosing between deliberation and voting for collective agreement does not have a single optimal strategy. The effectiveness of each approach is contingent upon specific, potentially competing epistemic goals such as truth, evidence, understanding, and epistemic justice.
detail.findings: The choice between group deliberation and voting is not inherently solved by a single strategy; it depends on the prioritization of different epistemic goals. [source-38394b50be99402b]
detail.limitations: The current evidence is limited to an abstract; it provides the theoretical framing but lacks the full arguments, model details, or empirical results that demonstrate the trade-offs between different epistemic goals.
detail.next_questions: Which formal models explicitly quantify the trade-offs between truth-conduciveness and epistemic justice in deliberative environments? How might voting protocols be modified to incorporate elements of epistemic justice?
detail.reason: Synthesizing the initial research phase into a provisional notebook to satisfy project requirements.

review.alternative: A singular, optimization-based approach might exist where all goals are reducible to a single objective function, though the source argues against this.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence of a unified formal framework that resolves these goals into a single metric without loss of information.

claims.statement: The choice between group deliberation and voting is not inherently solved by a single strategy; it depends on the prioritization of different epistemic goals.

support.explanation: The source explicitly states that the 'deliberation vs voting' choice depends on which epistemic goals the group prioritizes, rejecting the idea of a univocal 'best' strategy.
support.passage: We approach the deliberation versus voting question from a pluralist perspective, in that we hold that a group’s collective endeavor to solve an internal dispute can be aimed at different, albeit not necessarily incompatible, epistemic goals, namely the goals of truth, evidence, understanding, and epistemic justice. Different answers to our guiding question, we show, correspond with different epistemic goals.

review.alternative: A singular, optimization-based approach might exist where all goals are reducible to a single objective function, though the source argues against this.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence of a unified formal framework that resolves these goals into a single metric without loss of information.

support_provenance.statement: The choice between group deliberation and voting is not inherently solved by a single strategy; it depends on the prioritization of different epistemic goals.

nodes.title: Automated Detection of Objective Misspecification in Complex Systems

detail.title: Automated Detection of Objective Misspecification in Complex Systems
detail.summary: This revision integrates evidence on reward function divergence and the framing bottleneck in automated scientific inquiry.
detail.findings:
Reward maximization in biological and AI systems is prone to misspecification when the proxy signal diverges from the true objective. [source-c0b9aaa167024194]

The primary bottleneck for automated scientific progress lies in the formulation of the scientific objective rather than in answering questions. [source-6082c1cd1d7045f8]
detail.limitations: Findings are based on theoretical analysis of reward systems and preliminary observations on scientific inquiry bottlenecks; empirical data on failure mitigation is currently limited.
detail.next_questions: How can formal specification techniques be operationalized to detect divergence between reward signals and intended objectives in real-time?
detail.reason: Notebook updated to synthesize evidence regarding reward-based optimization limits and the framing bottleneck in automated research, satisfying the revision requirement for new evidence.

detail.summary: This notebook explores the hypothesis that episodic memory provides temporal continuity in autonomous agents, but persistent identity requires an integrative, potentially self-ethnographic layer that reconciles memory with internal regulatory invariants.

detail.limitations: Current evidence focuses on agent architectures and physical environmental interaction (Open Ant), lacking explicit comparative data on long-term self-model stability in the face of divergent memory streams.
detail.next_questions: Does the integration of a 'self-ethnographic' layer into agent architectures prevent the drift observed in simple reinforcement learning agents? How do we measure the emergence of an 'identity' versus mere 'state retention'?
